intro: Geetbets is a rural village in the east of Flemish Brabant, in the Hageland, on the border with Limburg. In its hamlet of Hulsbeek, beside the road to Halen, grows a sweet chestnut whose bark twists round the trunk in deep spiral furrows, with a plank bench on the grass in front of it. A reader photographed it and sent it to us; we do not yet know its age or girth.

trees.story:
In Hulsbeek, a hamlet of Geetbets on the quiet road to Halen, a reader stopped at this sweet chestnut and sent us a photograph from the grass beside it. They gave it no words, and the picture does not need many.

Look at the bark. On a sweet chestnut the furrows begin straight and, as the tree ages, start to twist, and on this trunk they run round it in long dark spirals from the roots to where it forks, as if the whole tree had been wrung slowly over many years. A rounded burr bulges from one side, the foot of the trunk swells out over the grass, and about a third of the way up great limbs leave it at wide angles to carry a crown that, in the reader's November photograph, is turning from green to gold. Someone has set a rough bench of thick planks on the grass facing it.

We do not know its girth or its age, or who planted a chestnut here in the Hageland, where oaks and poplars are the usual trees. If you know, or have measured it, tell us here and we will add your figures.

Sit on the bench and follow one furrow with your eye all the way up the trunk.

question_answer: The Sweet Chestnut of Hulsbeek stands on a grassy verge beside Weg op Halen in Hulsbeek, a hamlet of Geetbets in Flemish Brabant. It can be reached freely on foot.
question_context: A reader who passed through Hulsbeek, a hamlet of Geetbets in the east of Flemish Brabant, sent us a photograph of this sweet chestnut, which stands close to Weg op Halen, the road north towards Halen. The tree is worth the stop for its bark. A young sweet chestnut has straight furrows; an older one twists, and on this trunk the dark furrows wind round in long spirals from the roots up to the fork, where great limbs spread out to hold a broad crown. A rounded burr bulges from one side of the trunk and the base flares out over the grass. A rough bench made of thick planks stands facing it, so somebody local clearly likes it too. We have no measurement, planting date or register entry for it yet, so we give it no age. Sweet chestnuts are not native to Belgium and were planted for their nuts and timber, which means this one was put here by someone on purpose. If you know its story, tell us on the page and we will add it.
